back: Sinuses are imaged erect with a horizontal beam, specifically to demonstrate air-fluid levels. If the erect, horizontal-beam technique is not preserved, any fluid line disappears from the image.

front: Lateral sinus projection: CR entry point?
back: Erect, true lateral, CR horizontal, entering about 0.5 inch (1.25 cm) posterior to the outer canthus, showing all four sinus groups in profile.

front: Which horizontal-beam sinus projection is considered the workhorse view, and why?
back: The Waters method with a horizontal beam (chin on IR, OML at 37 degrees) best shows the maxillary sinuses, which is why it is the workhorse sinus projection.

front: AP axial cervical spine: CR angle and entry point?
back: CR angles 15 to 20 degrees cephalad, entering at C4 (thyroid cartilage level), demonstrating C3 through C7 and the disc spaces.

front: AP open-mouth odontoid: positioning and correct dens appearance?
back: The mouth opens fully so the occlusal plane and skull base are superimposed, CR perpendicular through the center of the open mouth. The dens should sit centered between the C1 lateral masses with equal space on each side.

front: Fuchs method: indication and positioning?
back: Used for the AP dens view when the patient cannot hold the mouth open and still. The neck is hyperextended until a line from the mentum to the mastoid tip is perpendicular to the IR, CR perpendicular just below the mandible tip.

front: Lateral cervical spine: SID, CR, and what must be visible on the image?
back: Usually erect at a long 72 inch (180 cm) SID, midsagittal plane parallel to the IR, shoulders relaxed and depressed, CR perpendicular entering at C4. All seven cervical vertebrae plus the C7-T1 junction must be shown, using gentle traction or weighted wrists if the shoulders obscure C7.

front: Swimmer's lateral: indication and technique?
back: Used to show the cervicothoracic junction (C7-T1) when the shoulders obscure it on a routine lateral. The arm nearer the IR raises overhead while the opposite shoulder depresses, CR horizontal, angled 3 to 5 degrees caudad, entering at T1.

front: PA oblique versus AP oblique cervical spine: which shows which foramina?
back: PA obliques best show the intervertebral foramina and pedicles closest to the IR, while AP obliques show those farthest from the IR. Both are taken at 45 degrees rotation, right and left.

front: When are cervical flexion and extension laterals performed, and when are they contraindicated?
back: They assess ligamentous stability with the chin tucked (flexion) or tilted back (extension), CR perpendicular at C4. They are never done in acute trauma until fracture is ruled out, since moving an unstable spine risks cord injury.

front: AP thoracic spine: breathing technique and CR?
back: Shallow, continuous breathing with a long exposure blurs ribs and lung markings while keeping the spine sharp. CR is perpendicular, entering about 3 to 4 inches (7 to 10 cm) below the jugular notch at T7.

front: Lateral thoracic spine: what are the two breathing approaches used, and why?
back: Shallow breathing blurs the lungs for the standard view, while full expiration is used for the lower thoracic vertebrae, since expiration elevates the diaphragm and reduces density over T10-T12.

front: What is the purpose and technique of the scoliosis series?
back: It measures spinal curvature for Cobb angle assessment, taken erect on a single long IR from C7 to the sacrum, PA or lateral, with no compression band and no angulation so the spine's natural alignment is preserved.

front: AP lumbar spine: positioning and CR?
back: Supine, knees flexed to flatten the lordotic curve, CR perpendicular entering at the iliac crest level (L4).

front: Lateral lumbar spine: positioning and CR?
back: True lateral, knees and hips flexed, a support placed under the waist to keep the spine parallel to the tabletop, CR perpendicular at the iliac crest (L4).

front: Why is a dedicated L5-S1 lateral spot view needed, and what is the CR angle?
back: The wings of the ilium often obscure L5-S1 on the routine lateral. A tightly collimated CR angles 5 to 8 degrees caudad, entering about 2 inches (5 cm) inferior and posterior to the iliac crest.

front: What do the lumbar oblique projections show, and which structures are best demonstrated closest to the IR?
back: They show the 'Scotty dog' appearance of the pars interarticularis, used to detect spondylolysis. On an anterior oblique (prone), structures closer to the IR are best shown; CR enters about 2 inches (5 cm) medial to the elevated side at L3.

front: AP axial L5-S1 projection: CR angle for males versus females?
back: Supine, CR angled 30 to 35 degrees cephalad for males or 35 to 40 degrees for females to compensate for a typically greater pelvic curve, entering midline superior to the pubic symphysis.

front: Sacrum and coccyx: why are they imaged as separate projections, and what are the CR angles?
back: Their curvature would foreshorten both on one straight AP. The AP axial sacrum angles the CR 15 degrees cephalad, entering about 2 inches (5 cm) superior to the pubic symphysis; the AP axial coccyx uses the opposite angle, 10 degrees caudad, from the same entry point.

front: Lateral sacrum and coccyx: CR entry point?
back: True lateral positioning, CR perpendicular entering about 3.5 inches (9 cm) posterior to the ASIS, roughly at the level of the greater trochanter.

front: AP axial sacroiliac (SI) joints: CR angle and entry?
back: Supine, CR angled 30 to 35 degrees cephalad, entering midline about 2 inches (5 cm) superior to the pubic symphysis, opening the naturally angled joint spaces.

front: Posterior oblique versus anterior oblique SI joint projections: which joint shows farther from the IR?
back: Posterior obliques (25 to 30 degrees from supine) show the SI joint farther from the table, CR entering about 1 inch (2.5 cm) medial to the elevated ASIS. Anterior obliques show the joint closer to the IR.

front: AP pelvis: leg positioning, why, and how does a correctly positioned image look?
back: Legs are internally rotated 15 to 20 degrees to correct for normal femoral anteversion and profile the femoral necks, CR perpendicular entering midline midway between the ASIS and pubic symphysis. A correct image shows symmetric iliac wings and obturator foramina, with the lesser trochanters minimal or absent since internal rotation tucks them behind the femoral shaft.

front: AP hip (unilateral): CR entry point?
back: Same internal leg rotation as the AP pelvis, centered and collimated to one hip. CR is perpendicular, entering about 1 inch (2.5 cm) inferior to a line from the ASIS to the pubic symphysis, at the femoral neck level.

front: Unilateral frog-leg lateral hip: what is it especially good for, and how is it positioned?
back: It is especially good for subtle femoral neck fractures or slipped capital femoral epiphysis in non-trauma patients. The hip and knee flex and the thigh abducts so the foot sole rests against the opposite knee, CR perpendicular at the femoral neck.

front: Danelius-Miller method: what is it and how is it performed?
back: It is the cross-table, horizontal-beam lateral hip used for suspected hip fracture. The unaffected leg is flexed and lifted out of the beam's path, the IR sits vertically against the lateral hip, and CR is directed horizontally, perpendicular to the femoral neck, entering the groin crease on the affected side, all without moving the injured leg.

front: Clements-Nakayama method: when is it used, and what is the CR angle?
back: Used when even the unaffected leg cannot be raised, or when both hips may be injured. The CR angles 15 to 20 degrees from horizontal, directed from below and lateral to the affected hip, entering at the femoral neck, without moving the injured leg.

front: Bilateral frog-leg pelvis: how is it positioned, and when is it commonly used?
back: Both legs are abducted, externally rotated, and knees flexed, comparing both hips at once. It is common in pediatric hip screening.

front: Inlet versus outlet AP axial pelvis views: CR angles and what each assesses?
back: The inlet view angles the CR 40 degrees caudad, entering midline about 2 inches (5 cm) below the ASIS level, assessing anteroposterior displacement of a pelvic ring injury. The outlet view angles the CR 35 to 40 degrees cephalad, entering midline at the pubic symphysis, assessing superior-inferior displacement.

front: Judet method: what is it, and what does it evaluate?
back: It is a posterior oblique acetabulum projection, rotating the patient 45 degrees posteriorly (both right and left are obtained), CR perpendicular entering about 2 inches (5 cm) inferior and 2 inches medial to the elevated ASIS. It evaluates the acetabular rims and columns after dislocation or fracture.

front: What is the purpose of an AP pelvis weight-bearing view?
back: It assesses pelvic ring stability and symphysis widening under physiologic load with the patient standing, an instability that a supine image cannot show.

front: What is the unifying trauma-imaging principle that explains cross-table laterals, the swimmer's lateral, and the Clements-Nakayama method?
back: Never move an injured part more than absolutely necessary. A horizontal beam or angled CR is used so the tube and IR do the work of achieving a diagnostic image instead of manipulating the patient.

front: On an AP or PA skull, spine, or pelvis image, what visual signature indicates rotation?
back: Asymmetric distance from the spinous processes to the pedicles on a spine image, or asymmetric obturator foramina and iliac wings on a pelvis image, both indicate rotation and require repositioning.

front: Where does the central ray enter for a PA chest radiograph?
back: Perpendicular to the midsagittal plane at the level of T7, roughly the inferior scapular angle.

front: Why does a PA projection beat an AP projection for chest imaging?
back: The heart sits anteriorly, so PA positioning keeps it closer to the receptor for a more accurate size, and standing upright lets the diaphragm drop so free fluid or free air settles where it is easiest to see.

front: What breathing instruction and rib count apply to a PA chest radiograph?
back: Full inspiration, with about ten posterior ribs visible above the diaphragm on a well-inflated image.

front: When is an AP chest projection used instead of PA?
back: When the patient cannot manage a PA, most often trauma or ICU patients; it is taken AP upright or AP supine, and the heart appears magnified in both.

front: Why is the left side placed against the receptor for a lateral chest?
back: The heart is left sided, so keeping the left side against the receptor keeps the heart closest to it and minimizes magnification.

front: What is the central ray placement and breathing instruction for a lateral chest?
back: Horizontal and perpendicular at T7 at the mid-coronal plane, taken on full inspiration with the arms raised overhead to clear the soft tissue.

front: What does the AP lordotic chest projection accomplish?
back: It throws the clavicles up and off the lung apices so the apices can be evaluated free of clavicular overlap.

front: How is the patient positioned for an AP lordotic chest projection?
back: Standing about a foot from the receptor and leaning back so the shoulders touch it while the body angles away; the central ray stays perpendicular to the receptor at T7.

front: For lateral decubitus chest positioning, which side goes down for a suspected pleural effusion and which side goes up for a suspected pneumothorax?
back: The affected side goes down for an effusion, since fluid pools to the dependent side, and the affected side goes up for a pneumothorax, since air rises.

front: How is rotation identified on a PA chest radiograph?
back: By comparing the distance from each sternoclavicular joint to the vertebral spinous process; unequal distances mean the patient was turned, which distorts heart size and mediastinal contours.

front: What breathing instruction is used for ribs above the diaphragm and why?
back: Full inspiration, positioned like a chest, because the air-filled lung provides the contrast needed to see the ribs clearly.

front: What breathing instruction is used for ribs below the diaphragm and why?
back: Full expiration, because raising the diaphragm out of the way keeps it from overlapping the lower ribs.

front: What is the purpose of rib oblique positioning?
back: RAO or LAO prone, or RPO or LPO supine, at about 45 degrees throws the axillary portion of the ribs into profile, clear of superimposition.

front: Why is the sternum imaged RAO instead of straight PA?
back: A straight PA sternum overlies the spine and heart; rotating 15 to 20 degrees from prone throws the sternum into the homogeneous heart shadow where it can be seen clearly.

front: What breathing technique is used for the RAO sternum and why?
back: Shallow breathing continued throughout the exposure, not suspended, which blurs the overlying ribs while the more rigid sternum stays sharp.

front: What must a lateral sternum radiograph show?
back: The whole sternum in profile without rib overlap, taken true lateral on full inspiration with the arms pulled back.

front: What is the central ray level for soft tissue neck radiographs, and why should the patient avoid phonating?
back: Perpendicular at the thyroid cartilage, around C6-C7; making a sound changes the airway's shape and position and would blur the structures being evaluated.

front: Why does a PA projection of the SC joints only work as a scout, and how is one joint isolated?
back: The SC joints sit over the spine on a PA, so it only shows both joints together; the RAO isolates the right joint and the LAO isolates the left, each with a 10 to 15 degree rotation.

front: What does the AP or PA axial clavicle projection add beyond the standard AP or PA clavicle?
back: Angling the central ray 15 to 30 degrees cephalad for AP or caudad for PA straightens the clavicle's natural curve and clears it of the ribs and scapula, since the straight AP or PA foreshortens that curve.

front: For PICC tip confirmation, where is the central ray directed and where must the tip terminate?
back: Central ray perpendicular at T7 on a portable AP chest, and the tip must terminate at the cavoatrial junction, where the superior vena cava meets the right atrium.

front: What is the central ray location, level, and breathing instruction for a KUB?
back: Perpendicular at the iliac crest, centering roughly L4-L5, exposed on expiration to reduce breathing motion.

front: What anatomy must be included on a KUB and why?
back: The diaphragm and the symphysis pubis both, since missing either edge could mean a free air or pelvic finding is missed.

front: Where is the central ray placed on an AP upright abdomen and why?
back: About two inches above the iliac crest to keep the diaphragm in the field, since both hemidiaphragms must be visible to catch free air.

front: Why is the patient positioned on the left side for a left lateral decubitus abdomen?
back: Free air rises over the liver on the left side down, where it shows up clearly against solid tissue rather than against the gas-filled stomach.

front: When is a dorsal decubitus abdomen used?
back: When the patient cannot lie on either side; it is taken supine with a horizontal beam from the side, central ray at the iliac crest along the midcoronal plane.

front: Why is the RAO the workhorse projection for an esophagram?
back: Rotating 35 to 40 degrees from prone clears the esophagus off the spine and heart shadow, with the central ray perpendicular at T5-T6.

front: What does the left lateral esophagram projection show?
back: The retrocardiac esophagus and any posterior indentation from an enlarged left atrium, at the same T5-T6 level.

front: How is a modified barium swallow performed?
back: Under live fluoroscopy with varied food and liquid consistencies, so positioning is directed moment to moment rather than following a fixed protocol.

front: Why must the patient be NPO at least eight hours before an upper GI series?
back: So the stomach is empty, since retained food dilutes contrast and can mimic pathology.

front: Why are patients asked to avoid smoking and gum chewing before an upper GI series?
back: Both stimulate gastric secretions and peristalsis that can wash barium off the mucosa before the images are taken.

front: What does the RAO projection demonstrate on an upper GI series?
back: The duodenal bulb and loop free of overlap, rotating 40 to 70 degrees from prone with the central ray at L1-L2.

front: What does the PA projection show on an upper GI series?
back: The stomach body, taken straight prone at L1-L2 on suspended expiration.

front: What does the right lateral projection show on an upper GI series?
back: The retrogastric space and duodenal bulb in profile, right side against the receptor at L1-L2.

front: Why is the LPO used on an upper GI series?
back: Barium sinks to the fundus while gas rises to the antrum and duodenal bulb as the patient is rotated left posterior, filling the fundus with barium, which is useful for double contrast studies.

front: What is the most common positioning error on the upper GI RAO and LPO obliques?
back: Under-rotating the body, which leaves the duodenal bulb or fundus still superimposed over the spine or antrum instead of clear of it.

front: How does a small bowel follow-through track barium?
back: A PA scout at L2 on suspended expiration is followed by PA images at timed intervals, commonly every 15 to 30 minutes, tracking the barium column through the jejunum and ileum.

front: Why are spot images with compression taken once contrast reaches the ileocecal valve?
back: To demonstrate the terminal ileum clearly, an area where Crohn disease findings are commonly sought.

front: Why does a contrast enema require thorough bowel prep beforehand?
back: So retained stool does not mimic a lesion and contrast coats the mucosa evenly.

front: What does the left lateral rectum projection evaluate on a contrast enema?
back: The rectosigmoid, taken before the rest of the colon fills, central ray perpendicular at the level of the ASIS, centered to the mid-coronal plane posterior to the ASIS, between the ASIS and the posterior sacrum.

front: What do the lateral decubitus views show on a contrast enema?
back: The medial and lateral colon walls, using the air-barium interface with a horizontal beam at the iliac crest.

front: Why are LPO and RPO used on a contrast enema?
back: To open the splenic and hepatic flexures, since they overlap each other on a straight AP.

front: What does the PA projection show on a contrast enema?
back: The transverse colon and both flexures together, central ray at the iliac crest.

front: What is the purpose of the axial sigmoid projection on a contrast enema, and what angle is used?
back: It unfolds the sigmoid loop, which otherwise hides polyps by overlapping itself, using a central ray angled 30 to 40 degrees caudad for PA or cephalad for AP.

front: What does a post-evacuation view on a contrast enema check?
back: Mucosal detail and how completely the colon empties, central ray perpendicular at the iliac crest.

front: What is the most common error during the double contrast air step of a contrast enema?
back: Losing rectal tube retention or over-insufflating, which either drains contrast prematurely and underfills the colon or distends it enough to flatten and hide polyps.

front: How is the patient positioned for surgical cholangiography, and what breathing instruction is given?
back: Positioning follows the surgical field, often a slight RAO to clear the duct off the spine; since the patient is under anesthesia, the anesthesiologist may briefly suspend ventilation instead of a direct breathing instruction.

front: How is the patient positioned during ERCP, and what is the radiographer's role?
back: Typically prone or semi-prone for endoscope access; the radiographer operates the fluoroscopic unit and takes spot images as directed by the gastroenterologist.

front: What anatomic coverage is required for a foreign body ingestion series?
back: Enough anatomy from the pharynx to the rectum, since the object can move well beyond where it was last seen.

front: What is the gold standard method for confirming feeding tube placement?
back: A portable AP chest or abdomen radiograph, which directly shows whether the tip has crossed the diaphragm into the stomach rather than coiling in the esophagus or entering the airway.

front: Why is breath suspended on every exposure during cystography?
back: Because motion blurs the bladder outline.

front: Why is the female voiding cystourethrogram taken AP?
back: The short, roughly 4-centimeter female urethra runs nearly straight down in the midline, so an AP view during voiding shows its full length without unfolding any curve.

front: Why is the male voiding cystourethrogram taken RPO instead of AP?
back: The longer male urethra curves through the prostatic and penile segments, and a 30 degree posterior oblique elongates and unfolds that curve so a stricture anywhere along it can be seen without foreshortening.

front: Why is breathing suspended on expiration for each exposure during retrograde urography?
back: Because the kidneys and ureters move with respiration.

front: When in the menstrual cycle is a hysterosalpingogram scheduled, and why?
back: In the first ten days of the cycle, after bleeding stops but before ovulation, to avoid an early pregnancy and get the clearest cavity image.

front: What does the AP scout accomplish before contrast is instilled for cystography?
back: It confirms there is no residual contrast in the bladder before filling, central ray perpendicular about two inches above the symphysis pubis.

front: PA hand: CR location and what the image must demonstrate
back: CR is perpendicular to the third metacarpophalangeal joint. The image must show the distal forearm through all phalanges with open joint spaces.

front: What is the fan lateral hand position and why is it used?
back: The fingers are spread like a fan so each digit clears its neighbor on the lateral projection. It is useful for showing anterior or posterior displacement of fracture fragments.

front: Why is the PA oblique hand rotated 45 degrees instead of taken flat?
back: Rotating 45 degrees with the fingers supported parallel to the IR opens the metacarpal spaces that overlap and superimpose on a straight PA view.

front: Isolated PA finger: CR location and technique
back: CR centers on the proximal interphalangeal joint of the affected digit, with the adjacent fingers flexed out of the way.

front: Why is a true lateral finger necessary in addition to the PA finger?
back: The lateral finger is critical for showing anterior or posterior displacement of a fracture fragment, which a PA projection would hide.

front: How is the AP thumb obtained?
back: The whole hand is rotated medially until the posterior surface of the thumb rests on the IR, with CR at the first MCP joint, giving a true AP of the digit.

front: How are the lateral and oblique thumb positions obtained?
back: The routine pronated PA hand position gives an oblique thumb for free, roughly 45 degrees from lateral, since the thumb's natural resting rotation relative to the fingers already places it obliquely. A true lateral thumb instead requires additional rotation beyond the routine PA hand position.

front: What is the purpose of ulnar deviation on a PA wrist projection?
back: In neutral position the scaphoid is foreshortened and can hide a fracture line. Deviating the wrist toward the ulna pulls the scaphoid away from the other carpals and elongates it, correcting the foreshortening.

front: Why is the scaphoid clinically significant among the carpal bones?
back: The scaphoid is the carpal bone most often fractured and is most prone to avascular necrosis if a fracture is missed.

front: What is the Stecher method and why is it used?
back: The Stecher method is a PA axial scaphoid projection that adds a 20 to 25 degree proximal CR angle with the wrist still in ulnar deviation, elongating the scaphoid even further than ulnar deviation alone to clear a fracture line.

front: What is the Gaynor-Hart method and what does it demonstrate?
back: The Gaynor-Hart method is a tangential carpal canal projection that hyperextends the wrist palm up with CR angled 25 to 30 degrees along the hand's long axis into the carpal canal. It demonstrates the pisiform, the hamulus of the hamate, and the tunnel that carpal tunnel syndrome affects.

front: What is a bone age study and what does it use for comparison?
back: A single PA of the left hand and wrist is compared against a standardized reference atlas, classically Greulich and Pyle, to estimate skeletal maturity. It is useful for evaluating growth disorders or predicting adult height.

front: PA, lateral, and oblique wrist: CR location
back: CR is centered at the midcarpal area for the standard PA, lateral, and oblique wrist projections.

front: Forearm AP: positioning and why
back: The arm is fully extended with the hand supinated so the radius and ulna lie parallel without crossing, CR at the mid-forearm, with both the wrist and elbow joints included.

front: Why does a true lateral forearm require the thumb-up position?
back: The elbow is flexed 90 degrees with the hand thumb-up because that position keeps the radius and ulna from overlapping, which is required for a true lateral.

front: Elbow AP: positioning and what it demonstrates
back: The arm is extended with the hand supinated, CR perpendicular to the joint, demonstrating the joint space free of superimposition along with the proximal radius, ulna, and distal humerus.

front: Lateral elbow: flexion angle and CR
back: The elbow is flexed exactly 90 degrees with the hand thumb-up, CR directed at the joint.

front: On a correctly positioned lateral elbow, what do the anterior and posterior fat pads indicate?
back: The anterior fat pad is normally a faint visible sliver. The posterior fat pad is normally invisible, and its appearance signals a joint effusion, often from an occult fracture.

front: Medial oblique elbow: rotation and what it best shows
back: The arm is rotated about 45 degrees medially, best demonstrating the coronoid process.

front: Lateral oblique elbow: rotation and what it best shows
back: The arm is rotated about 45 degrees laterally, best demonstrating the radial head, neck, and capitulum.

front: When is the AP partial flexion technique used at the elbow, and how is it performed?
back: It is used when a patient cannot fully extend the elbow. Two exposures are taken, one centered on the distal humerus and one on the proximal forearm, each with CR entering wherever that segment sits closest to the IR, avoiding forced extension that a possible fracture makes unsafe.

front: What is the Coyle method and when is it used?
back: The Coyle method uses trauma axial laterals of the elbow when even partial flexion is not tolerated. With the elbow flexed near 90 degrees, it works around whatever limited motion the elbow allows.

front: Coyle method: what do the two CR angles each demonstrate?
back: One exposure angles CR 45 degrees toward the shoulder, showing the radial head, neck, and capitulum, useful for radial head fractures. The second angles CR 45 degrees toward the hand, showing the coronoid process and trochlea, useful for coronoid process fractures.

front: Why is the humerus AP taken in neutral rotation when a fracture is suspected?
back: Forcing rotation of the arm risks displacing fracture fragments, so the epicondyles are kept parallel to the IR without rotating the arm.

front: What is the transthoracic lateral humerus and when is it used?
back: It is used for a trauma patient instead of a rotational lateral. The injured arm hangs at the side, the other arm raises overhead, and CR passes horizontally through the thorax to project a true lateral without moving the injured arm.

front: Why does the transthoracic lateral humerus use a breathing technique?
back: Shallow breathing during a longer low-mA exposure blurs the ribs and lungs while the denser humerus stays comparatively sharp, since it is one of the few extremity views where breathing technique matters.

front: AP shoulder internal rotation vs external rotation: what does each profile?
back: Internal rotation turns the palm posteriorly, profiling the lesser tuberosity medially. External rotation turns the palm anteriorly, profiling the greater tuberosity laterally and giving the clearest view of the humeral head.

front: Why is arm rotation avoided when a shoulder fracture or dislocation is suspected?
back: Rotating the arm can worsen the injury, which is exactly why the AP neutral rotation and other trauma-specific shoulder views exist.

front: What is the AP neutral rotation shoulder used for?
back: It leaves the arm exactly as the patient presents it and serves as the safe first trauma view when fracture or dislocation is suspected.

front: What is the Grashey method and why is it the standard for suspected dislocation?
back: The Grashey method is a posterior oblique shoulder rotated 35 to 45 degrees from a true AP with the affected side against the IR. Rotating the scapula's flat surface parallel to the IR aligns the beam tangent to the glenohumeral joint, opening the joint space cleanly, which is why it is standard for suspected dislocation or joint narrowing.

front: Why does a straight AP shoulder fail to show the glenohumeral joint space clearly?
back: The glenoid fossa faces anterolaterally rather than straight forward, so a straight AP beam catches the glenoid at a slant and causes it to overlap the humeral head.

front: What is the Lawrence method and what does it demonstrate?
back: The Lawrence method is an inferosuperior axial projection showing the humeral head-glenoid relationship from below, useful for posterior dislocation. The arm abducts 90 degrees if possible, with CR angled 25 to 30 degrees medially through the axilla.

front: What is the scapular Y view and why is it valuable in trauma?
back: The patient is positioned at roughly a 60 degree anterior oblique with the affected shoulder against the IR, so the scapular body, coracoid, and acromion form a Y with the humeral head normally centered at the junction. Since no arm movement is needed, it is valuable in trauma.

front: How does the scapular Y view distinguish anterior from posterior shoulder dislocation?
back: The humeral head is displaced toward whichever arm of the Y corresponds to the direction of dislocation, rather than sitting centered at the junction.

front: What is the Neer method and what does it evaluate?
back: The Neer method is a supraspinatus outlet view, a steeper version of the scapular Y angled 10 to 15 degrees caudad, profiling the outlet space for evaluating impingement.

front: AP and lateral scapula: positioning and CR
back: The AP scapula abducts the arm 90 degrees to draw the scapula off the ribs, CR at the mid-scapular body, sometimes with a breathing technique to blur lung markings. The lateral scapula uses the same oblique body rotation as the scapular Y view.

front: How are AC joints imaged and why are two exposures taken?
back: Both AC joints are imaged bilaterally on one long IR, AP, CR at the midline at joint level. Two exposures are taken, one without weights and one with weights suspended, to reveal a separation the unstressed view might miss.

front: Why are AC joint stress weights suspended rather than held by the patient?
back: Gripping a weight recruits shoulder muscles, which can mask a separation, so the weight is suspended from the wrist instead.

front: AP entire forefoot: CR location and purpose
back: CR centers at the third metatarsophalangeal joint, showing all five toes and distal metatarsals as a screening view.

front: Individual AP or AP axial toe: CR location
back: CR centers on that digit's interphalangeal joint (the sole IP joint on the two-phalanx great toe, or the proximal interphalangeal joint on toes two through five), sometimes angled slightly to open the joint on a short great toe.

front: Oblique toe and lateral toe: how are they obtained and why is the lateral needed?
back: The oblique toe rotates the foot 30 to 45 degrees medially. The lateral toe isolates the affected digit with the other toes taped away, needed to show displacement an AP view cannot.

front: AP axial foot: CR angle and why it is angled
back: CR angles 10 degrees toward the heel, entering the base of the third metatarsal, compensating for the foot's natural arch so the tarsometatarsal joints are not foreshortened.

front: Medial oblique foot: rotation and clinical role
back: The foot rotates 30 degrees medially, opening the sinus tarsi and separating the metatarsal bases. It is the standard oblique for foot trauma.

front: Lateral foot: CR location
back: CR is directed at the base of the third metatarsal on a true mediolateral projection, showing the arch profile.

front: Why are weight-bearing foot views ordered?
back: They are taken standing for arch collapse, flatfoot, or hardware alignment under physiologic load, since a supine image cannot show how the arch behaves under body weight.

front: Lateral calcaneus: CR location
back: CR enters about one inch inferior to the medial malleolus on a straightforward mediolateral projection.

front: Plantodorsal axial calcaneus: CR angle and why it is so steep
back: CR angles 40 degrees cephalad into the plantar surface of the heel. The steep angle is needed to project the calcaneal body clear of the talus and lower leg above it.

front: AP ankle: positioning and its main limitation
back: The leg is extended with the foot dorsiflexed, CR perpendicular midway between the malleoli, showing the distal tibia, fibula, and talus, though the joint space is not fully open because the fibula overlaps the talus slightly.

front: Mortise ankle view: how much rotation and why is it needed?
back: The foot and leg are internally rotated 15 to 20 degrees. The two malleoli are not in the same coronal plane, so this rotation brings the intermalleolar line parallel to the IR and places CR perpendicular to the actual joint.

front: What does a correctly positioned mortise view show?
back: It shows an even joint space around all three sides of the talus with no fibula-tibia overlap, and any narrowing or widening signals ligament injury or fracture that a plain AP would miss.

front: Lateral ankle: CR location and use
back: CR is directed at the medial malleolus on a mediolateral projection, showing the tibiotalar joint from the side and useful for displacement or effusion.

front: Medial oblique ankle: how does it differ from the mortise view?
back: The medial oblique ankle rotates 45 degrees medially, profiling the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis, a larger rotation than the mortise view's 15 to 20 degrees. Both rotate the same direction but serve different purposes at different angles.

front: AP stress views of the ankle: what do they evaluate?
back: Manual inversion or eversion is applied during exposure to evaluate ligament laxity against a normal side.

front: Why are weight-bearing AP and lateral ankle views ordered?
back: They are taken standing to evaluate alignment and joint narrowing under load, often for chronic instability or syndesmotic injury.

front: Tibia-fibula AP and lateral: why are both adjacent joints included?
back: Both the knee and ankle are included with CR at the mid-shaft, since shaft fractures can accompany injury at either adjacent joint.

front: AP knee: CR location and when is it angled cephalad?
back: CR is perpendicular, entering about half an inch below the patellar apex, or angled 3 to 5 degrees cephalad in a larger body habitus, since greater lordotic tilt otherwise foreshortens the joint space.

front: Why are weight-bearing AP knee views ordered?
back: Standing on both legs evaluates joint space narrowing from osteoarthritis, since cartilage loss only shows under load and a supine image can look deceptively normal.

front: Lateral knee: flexion angle and CR direction
back: The knee flexes 20 to 30 degrees, CR angled 5 to 7 degrees cephalad, directed below the medial epicondyle.

front: Why is the lateral knee not flexed further than 20 to 30 degrees?
back: Flexing further tightens the joint and can hide a suprapatellar effusion, a key finding this view is meant to catch.

front: Medial and lateral knee obliques: what do they clear and evaluate?
back: Rotating 45 degrees each way clears the femoral condyles and tibial plateau of overlap and evaluates the fibular head.

front: What is the general purpose of the intercondylar fossa (tunnel) views of the knee?
back: They show the notch between the femoral condyles for osteochondral defects and loose bodies.

front: What is the Holmblad method?
back: The Holmblad method is a PA axial intercondylar fossa projection with the patient kneeling, knee flexed about 70 degrees, CR perpendicular to the lower leg, which because of that steep flexion enters the fossa nearly straight through.

front: What is the Camp Coventry method and when is it chosen?
back: The Camp Coventry method is a PA axial intercondylar fossa projection done prone, knee flexed 40 to 50 degrees, CR angled 40 to 50 degrees caudad to match the flexion. It is chosen when kneeling is not tolerated.

front: What is the Béclère method?
back: The Béclère method is the supine alternative for the intercondylar fossa, knee flexed 40 to 45 degrees on a sponge, CR angled 40 to 45 degrees cephalad to match, so the beam travels straight through the notch regardless of patient position.

front: What is the Merchant method and why are both knees imaged together?
back: The Merchant method is a tangential patellofemoral projection taken supine with both knees flexed 40 degrees off the table end, CR angled 30 degrees from the long axis of the legs. Both knees are imaged together for side-to-side comparison of subluxation or tracking.

front: What is the Settegast method and why is it used less often today?
back: The Settegast method is a tangential patellofemoral projection taken prone with the knee flexed as sharply as tolerated, CR angled 15 to 20 degrees cephalad into the joint. It is used less often since forced sharp flexion can displace a suspected patellar fracture.

front: Why is the standalone PA patella taken prone?
back: The prone position brings the patella closer to the IR, with CR perpendicular exiting the patella, improving detail.

front: Femur AP and lateral: which joint is included?
back: One adjacent joint, hip or knee, is generally included depending on where the pathology is suspected, with the opposite joint imaged separately if the femur is too long for one IR.

front: What is a scanogram and how is it performed?
back: A scanogram, or long bone measurement, evaluates limb length discrepancy. A radiopaque ruler is placed alongside the limb, and three separate exposures are taken on one long IR, each centered individually over the hip, knee, and ankle with CR perpendicular to that joint.

front: Why does a scanogram use three separate centered exposures instead of one exposure down the whole leg?
back: Centering each joint separately avoids the magnification distortion a single divergent beam would cause, since a joint far from CR would appear artificially larger or smaller than one centered directly under it, corrupting the measurement.

front: When is a skeletal survey ordered for metastatic disease screening?
back: It is ordered in adults since cancers such as breast, prostate, and lung commonly spread to bone, and a survey of the skull, spine, ribs, pelvis, and long bones can catch lytic or sclerotic lesions before a pathologic fracture occurs.

front: What is a child abuse skeletal survey and why does it image each extremity individually?
back: It is a suspected non-accidental trauma workup in a young child. Inflicted injuries often include fractures at different healing stages that are not clinically obvious, so a full survey imaging the skull, chest, spine, pelvis, and each extremity individually documents every skeletal injury present, including old healed fractures the history omits.

front: What is arthrography and what does it show that plain radiographs cannot?
back: Arthrography is a fluoroscopically or ultrasound-guided procedure injecting contrast, either iodinated contrast alone or iodinated contrast plus air, directly into a joint capsule to outline soft tissue such as the capsule lining, cartilage, ligaments, and the menisci or labrum.

front: When is direct MR arthrography still used despite MRI largely replacing conventional arthrography?
back: Direct MR arthrography, injecting dilute gadolinium into the joint before scanning, is still used when the extra distension improves visualization of a subtle labral or ligament tear.

front: What is the difference between joint aspiration and joint injection?
back: Joint aspiration withdraws fluid for diagnostic testing such as infection or gout, or for therapeutic relief of a painful effusion. Joint injection instead delivers a corticosteroid and local anesthetic to reduce inflammation and pain, typically guided by fluoroscopy or ultrasound.
